Transcript:
[00:00] Evan Brooks: okay good afternoon everyone, thanks for carving out time. quick check in — we'll go 45 minutes and then wrap, sound good?
[00:07] Aisha Rahman: yeah that's perfect, we have about the same window. thanks Evan.
[00:11] Priya Malhotra: hi all, i'll lead the integration bits, jonas is on for dev adv notes. we pulled the logs from last week's run, there's a couple of odd fails when the tool call returns 502s.
[00:21] Tom Grover: yeah we saw that, and also bursts where latency spikes to 700-900ms on 512-token prompts, which breaks our UI Aha — so want to get a reliable fallback.
[00:31] Jonas Lee: quick Q, are you preferring hosted for the pilot or already leaning dedicated? just to frame tuning.
[00:36] Aisha Rahman: pilot is hosted to start, but if the throughput is variable we might shift to Dedicated; cost is a factor though.
[00:44] Evan Brooks: understood. for hosted you get fastest onboarding — we can enable model pinning and region routing in the SDK. for dedicated we'd recommend reserved pools with burst capacity; that gives predictable p95 and you avoid noisy neighbor issues.
[00:55] Tom Grover: when you say model pinning, is that per-route? like we have multiply routes for summarize vs redaction vs clinical-extract.
[01:02] Priya Malhotra: yes per-route model + version. the SDK config looks like a per-route policy block — you can set fallback models, latency SLOs, and cost-tier so the router will choose cheaper variants if under load.
[01:15] Tom Grover: sounds good, can you show the snippet?
[01:18] Priya Malhotra: (link shared) here's an example — // pseudo code — sdk.route('clinical-extract').pin({model: 'open-llm-med-v2', fallback: 'open-llm-med-v2-qa'}) — also shows circuit breaker and backoff hooks. we'll send a cleaned snippet after.
[01:34] Aisha Rahman: quick question on the fallback — will the output contract be stable if we switch to the fallback model? we depend on structured JSON fields.
[01:42] Priya Malhotra: great Q — we recommend schema-driven prompts + a post-parse validation layer. also you can set model families in catalog so fallbacks are chosen from models trained for similar output formats. but we did see some noise, so you should validate server-side and have an optional re-run strategy.
[01:58] Tom Grover: Re-run would add latency though, how do teams usually balance that?
[02:03] Evan Brooks: common pattern: optimistic first pass then async re-eval. UI shows interim payload, while server triggers a higher-quality job and replaces when done. depends on UX tolerance.
[02:13] Hiro Tanaka: what about function/tool calling? we have external validators and a redaction tool that we call as part of the flow. sometimes the tool is slow or rate-limited.
[02:21] Priya Malhotra: we see two patterns: 1) synchronous tool calls where the model calls a service and waits — best when tools are stable and low-latency; 2) async tool orchestration where the model emits a structured call and a worker handles it, and then you reconcile. async is safer for flaky tools.
[02:37] Tom Grover: we currently do sync to keep UX snappy, but maybe a hybrid? do you have examples for graceful degradation?
[02:43] Jonas Lee: yes — e.g., SDK timeout at 1.2s, if no response then fallback to a cached answer or a smaller model for hallucination-restricted extraction, and mark result as partial in the JSON payload. we've seen that reduce error surface significantly.
[02:58] Rita Soliman: on security — we need to know how keys are managed. KMS integration, also audit logs for each model call, and data residency.
[03:07] Evan Brooks: Redwood Private supports KMS/HSM and you can route telemetry logs to your SIEM. hosted retains logs for 30 days by default; enterprise retention and audit exports are configurable. we'll include SOC 2 docs and the KMS integration guide in the follow-up.
[03:22] Rita Soliman: okay, can you confirm whether RBAC is available per-route? we want least-privilege for data access.
[03:27] Priya Malhotra: yes RBAC and token-scoped policies — you can issue per-service tokens with route-level bindings and duration. we'll include a short checklist.
[03:34] Aisha Rahman: back to performance — Priya, you mentioned KV or prefix cache as an approach. can you explain how that would work for our extract route?
[03:41] Priya Malhotra: sure — prefix/KV caching stores the past KV cache entries for similar prompts. if your clinical-extract calls have repeated headers or boilerplate, caching the KV can avoid regenerating attention states for the initial tokens. practically you see big wins when sequence reuse is high. when you have unique patient notes every time the hit rate drops.
[03:58] Tom Grover: matches our case maybe 30% repeat patterns. do you have numbers from other customers?
[04:03] Priya Malhotra: on similar ER-note workloads we've seen token cost drop 20-40% and p95 drop ~15-30% after enabling aggressive prefix caching and batching. but you'll need to tune cache TTL and invalidation for PHI safety.
[04:17] Hiro Tanaka: PHI safety — caching patient data is sensitive, so what's the recommended approach?
[04:22] Priya Malhotra: store only hashed or anonymized keys and never persist raw PHI in external caches; if you deploy Private we can keep KV on your VPC and apply KMS encryption. for hosted we recommend short TTLs and opt-in retention with encryption-at-rest. Rita, we'll sync on specifics for SOC 2 scope.
[04:39] Rita Soliman: yes pls. also need to know how to audit cache evictions.
[04:43] Evan Brooks: endpoint emits cache event logs and we can ship them to your SIEM — detail that in security doc.
[04:48] Aisha Rahman: about telemetry — we want per-request token breakdowns and model-level latencies, not aggregated. is that possible?
[04:55] Jonas Lee: yep, Redwood Console exposes per-route token counts and token level cost; you can also stream traces to Jaeger/OTel. we'll share a dashboard template.
[05:04] Tom Grover: earlier you said router chooses cheaper variants — can we configure cost floors so we never go below a quality bar?
[05:11] Priya Malhotra: absolutely — policy allows quality thresholds (e.g., BLEU/semantic score proxies) and will only pick fallback models if predicted quality is above threshold. it's heuristic, but combined with your unit tests it works well.
[05:23] Aisha Rahman: Tom and I ran the smoke tests last night; one oddity was structured output sometimes had extra fields or nulls in array positions.
[05:32] Tom Grover: yeah that caused our schema parser to choke.
[05:36] Priya Malhotra: two mitigations — 1) strict schema validation with a reject-or-rewrite policy, 2) use function calling to constrain output to exact JSON fields. function calling tends to be more deterministic but you do trade off verbosity.
[05:52] Hiro Tanaka: can you give an example of a function call for a clinical-extract where the model returns an array of findings?
[05:57] Priya Malhotra: sure — model emits function name extractFindings with params {patient_id, findings:[{label, location, confidence}]} — the SDK will validate types and reject malformed items, then you can surface errors. we'll send example schema.
[06:11] Aisha Rahman: that looks promising. question: if the function call fails because the worker times out, how do you want us to handle reconciliation?
[06:19] Jonas Lee: recommended pattern: mark as pending, persist a partial result and queue a re-run with higher timeout on a worker pool. you can also include a provenance object in the JSON with status flags so UI knows it's incomplete.
[06:30] Tom Grover: circling back to error obs — we saw 502s specifically when the validator service returned upstream 504s; is it better to move validator to async to avoid cascading failures?
[06:40] Priya Malhotra: yes async decouples the critical path. for low-latency UX you can do a fast pass with heuristics then run the heavy validator async and patch results.
[06:49] Rita Soliman: about logs retention — hosted 30 days is okay for pilot but we will need longer for post-prod. what's the pricing?
[06:56] Evan Brooks: we'll include retention add-on pricing in the follow-up; generally it's usage-based plus flat storage fee for long-term retention.
[07:04] Aisha Rahman: great. any blockers on our side for the next run?
[07:08] Tom Grover: we'll need the SDK snippet and the sample circuit-breaker. also we'll re-run with larger concurrency.
[07:15] Evan Brooks: ok we'll deliver those.
[07:18] Priya Malhotra: quick note on telemetry instrumentation — include request-id propagation from your frontend through the SDK; it makes tracing root cause trivial.
[07:28] Tom Grover: good call. we'll add that.
[07:31] Aisha Rahman: another quick thing — is there any recommended tokenization setting for clinical text? we saw costs vary a bit.
[07:38] Jonas Lee: tokenizer choice is model-specific; but for notes we see slightly fewer tokens with the 'med-bpe' tokenizers. we'll include recommended tokenizer settings for the pinned model.
[07:47] Hiro Tanaka: can you confirm whether the SDK supports per-request metadata headers for PII flags? we want to mark certain requests with higher retention rules.
[07:56] Priya Malhotra: yes you can send metadata and tags; Console will store them with the trace. we can also route those to a dedicated retention policy.
[08:04] Rita Soliman: good. security question — if we go Dedicated on-prem, can we use our HSM for signing?
[08:10] Evan Brooks: yep Dedicated and Private supports HSM/KMS integration and you keep keys in your vault. we'll capture the integration steps in the doc.
[08:18] Aisha Rahman: ok moving toward next steps, what does Redwood need from us to run the KV baseline?
[08:23] Priya Malhotra: ideally a sample corpus (anonymized) or at least token patterns plus target concurrency. we'll give a runbook — Tom you'll run the harness and upload results.
[08:33] Tom Grover: I'll do 1k concurrency and incremental run 100/250/500/1k.
[08:37] Evan Brooks: perfect — add the run times and the p50/p95/p99 numbers. we'll compare against our baseline and suggest tuning.
[08:45] Aisha Rahman: timeline — we aim to decide by March 23 whether to keep hosted or switch Dedicated for phase 2.
[08:52] Evan Brooks: sounds reasonable. we'll surface estimated costs for both paths.
[08:55] Priya Malhotra: one last practical — function calling failure modes: sometimes the model invents fields. we recommend strict field-level validators; show partial results to product and re-run if confidence low.
[09:07] Hiro Tanaka: makes sense. thanks.
[09:10] Evan Brooks: ok let's recap next steps — we'll share: SDK routing snippet + circuit breaker, function-calling schema examples, security docs for KMS/SOC2, and a benchmark runbook. Nexa to run KV baseline and list constraints.
[09:25] Aisha Rahman: thanks all. we'll target those due dates.
[09:29] Evan Brooks: great, closing now.
